rationale: Start with a broad gradient to locate the eight-compound elution window and identify critical pairs while minimizing the risk of missing strongly retained compounds. A moderate temperature leaves room to probe temperature-dependent selectivity in subsequent injections.
Only the first pair needs improvement, while every other pair has substantial resolution margin. Raising temperature tests selectivity for that pair and should keep the last peak below 10 minutes.
Lengthen the gradient at the same temperature to measure the critical first pair’s response to slope. The current time margin should accommodate this change with the last peak near 10 minutes.

The first pair needs only a small resolution gain, and raising temperature previously improved its separation. Increasing to 60 C should also shorten retention, offering a strong chance of full resolution with the last peak before 10 minutes.

Injection 4 reached the maximum CRF, so now test a shorter gradient while preserving full resolution. Reducing tG by one grid step should shorten elution with a reasonable margin at both closest pairs.

Shorten the gradient another grid step to reduce analysis time while targeting the maximum CRF. The first pair’s trend predicts resolution around 1.7, while the other close pair improved with the previous shortening.

Shorten the gradient while lowering its endpoint so the slope increases only modestly, aiming to keep the first pair above R = 1.5. The last peak previously eluted near 0.56 organic fraction, leaving ample endpoint strength for complete elution.

Shift the gradient window upward at unchanged slope to test whether initial solvent strength can shorten retention while preserving the critical first pair. Injection 7 remains the fastest demonstrated method with maximum CRF.

Probe the low-temperature selectivity regime, where the critical early pair may separate in the opposite elution order. A steeper gradient offsets the increased retention and tests a potentially faster route to full resolution.

Raise temperature one step to test whether the late three-peak cluster separates while retaining the early pair’s low-temperature resolution. Keeping the gradient unchanged isolates temperature-dependent selectivity.

Test a higher starting organic fraction to shorten the low-temperature method and alter early-pair selectivity. Raising temperature to 35 C should further separate the late cluster, while the narrower gradient window provides a shallower slope.

Return to the fully resolved high-temperature regime and trim the endpoint while shortening the gradient. The slope is only slightly steeper than injection 7, targeting a modestly shorter elution time with the first pair still above R = 1.5.

Test a slightly steeper gradient, near the predicted R = 1.5 boundary for the first pair. The last peak may enter the final hold, so this run will determine whether the shorter gradient actually reduces elution time while preserving maximum CRF.

Test whether a shallower slope restores full resolution at the higher starting organic fraction that failed in injection 8. This brackets the slope–starting-strength tradeoff, while injection 13 remains the fastest demonstrated maximum-CRF method.

Test a substantially steeper gradient in the low-temperature regime to see whether slope-dependent selectivity breaks up the late cluster seen in injection 9. This explores a faster alternative while retaining injection 13 as the fastest proven fully resolved method.

Test a slope of 0.085 organic fraction per minute, just above the fastest fully resolved slope demonstrated so far. This should locate the first pair’s resolution boundary and determine whether elution can be shortened further without sacrificing maximum CRF.

Test whether a shallower gradient restores the early pair’s resolution at 35 C, while a higher starting organic fraction offsets the added retention time. The late cluster was already resolved at this temperature in injection 11.

Lower the starting organic fraction to retain the early pair more strongly, using an intermediate slope to limit total retention. This tests whether the 35 C regime can achieve maximum CRF as an alternative to the established 60 C methods.

Reduce the slope one grid step from injection 18 to bring its first pair above R = 1.5. The last peak should remain below 10 minutes, potentially establishing a fully resolved, maximum-CRF alternative at lower temperature.

The maximum CRF is already established; this run targets greater resolution margin by balancing the two closest pairs with a slope between injections 4 and 5. Trimming the endpoint to 0.65 should keep all peaks within the gradient and the last peak below 10 minutes.

Shift the balanced high-temperature method to a higher starting organic fraction and slightly steeper slope to shorten retention. This tests whether full resolution with a larger safety margin than injection 13 can be retained in a trimmed eight-minute gradient.

Shorten injection 20 by one gradient-time step, targeting full resolution with less analysis time. This matches injection 6’s successful slope but trims the unused high-organic portion, with the last peak expected before the gradient ends.

Test a higher starting organic fraction with a shallower slope to compensate for the early pair’s loss of retention. This checks the remaining starting-strength tradeoff while preserving injection 13 as the fastest demonstrated maximum-CRF method.

Test a slope just above injection 14’s fully resolved boundary at phi0 = 0.10, aiming to shorten elution while keeping the first pair at R ≥ 1.5. Injection 13 remains the fastest proven maximum-CRF method.

Use the final injection to refine resolution margin at the already-achieved maximum CRF, with a slope between injections 5 and 20 predicted to balance both critical pairs near R = 2. Injection 13 remains the fastest demonstrated fully resolved method.
